questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of <Link> over a plain <a> for internal navigation?

options.text: It navigates client-side without a full page reload, and prefetches the route
It only works for external URLs
It disables JavaScript for that page

questions.explanation: <Link> does fast client-side navigation and prefetches linked routes in production, while a plain <a> reloads the entire page.

questions.prompt: In the App Router, from which module do you import useRouter and usePathname? Type the module path.
questions.explanation: App Router navigation hooks come from next/navigation. next/router is the old Pages Router module.

questions.prompt: Which of these require a Client Component ("use client")? Select all that apply.

options.text: A basic <Link href> with no hooks

questions.explanation: usePathname and useRouter are hooks and need a Client Component. redirect() runs on the server, and a plain <Link> works anywhere.

questions.prompt: How do you navigate to /checkout from a button's onClick handler?
questions.explanation: In a Client Component, useRouter() gives you push() for programmatic navigation. redirect() is for server code, not click handlers.

questions.prompt: Match each navigation tool to its purpose.
questions.explanation: <Link> is declarative, useRouter navigates from logic, usePathname reads the path, and redirect() runs on the server.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when a prefetched <Link> is clicked.

items.text: The link scrolls into view and Next.js prefetches the route
Next.js renders the already-loaded route in place
The URL updates without a full page reload

questions.explanation: Links prefetch when visible; clicking then swaps in the route client-side and updates the URL with no full reload.
